# AI Film Master Guide — full text

Static site: site/index.html. API: api/v1/. Generated 2026-10-11.

<!-- chapter: higgsfield/platform-mastery.md -->
# Higgsfield Platform Mastery

## The model roster (what to use when)

Higgsfield is model-agnostic — it hosts many engines under one credit pool. Third-party model guides rank them this way (tiers: Free / Low 0.1–2 credits / Mid 2–10 / Premium 10+):

| Need | Model | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| Top-tier cinematic video + native audio | Kling 3.0 | Premium |
| Epic scale / spectacle | Sora 2 | Premium |
| Nature / landscapes + reference images | Veo 3.1 | Premium |
| Artistic / stylized video | Wan 2.6 | Mid |
| Fast iteration | Seedance 2.0 Pro | Mid |
| VFX / fluid motion | Minimax Hailuo 2.3 | Mid |
| Budget-friendly video | Kling 2.5 Turbo / Higgsfield DoP Lite | Free–Low |

Image side: Soul 2.0 (fashion/aesthetic, free), Soul Cinema (cinematic stills with film grain and era-aware styling), Nano Banana Pro (photorealistic, low cost), Soul Cast (AI actor generation).

**Key insight:** a clip made through Higgsfield on the Kling engine is a Kling clip — what differs is how you buy it (shared credit pool) and what you can steer (presets vs raw prompt control). Going to Kling directly exposes controls Higgsfield's preset UI hides: end-frame pinning, multi-reference `elements`, multi-prompt shots, 3–15s durations.

## Cinema Studio — the filmmaking layer

Cinema Studio is Higgsfield's director-mode workspace:

- **Camera movement controls:** static, handheld, zoom, pan, dolly, orbit and more — several moves can be stacked in one shot
- **Genre settings:** Action, Epic, Drama, Comedy, Horror — the whole scene follows the genre's look and pacing
- **Era selection:** regrade to look like the 1960s, 1980s, 1990s, or today
- **AI Cast:** build custom AI actors with chosen look, outfit, era, personality
- **Scene building:** place locations and props, shape the frame
- **Emotions:** choose what each character shows
- **Color grading:** fine-tune color, temperature, contrast, presets
- **Multiple references:** upload many reference images to guide generation
- **Real-time co-directing:** invite teammates onto one project
- **AI assistant:** help with camera angles, lighting, prompts, script-to-shot breakdowns

It isn't tied to one model — pick the best engine per shot.

## Generation controls that matter

- **Start frame:** upload or generate the opening image; the clip grows from it. This is the single biggest quality lever.
- **End frame** (where supported): pin exactly where a camera move finishes — turns drift into intention.
- **Camera movement presets:** faster than prompt engineering; pick the move, don't describe it.
- **Duration:** longer clips cost more and drift more. Short, locked shots chain better than long wandering ones.
- **Aspect ratio:** match your delivery format from the first generation, never crop later.

## Turbo vs Standard thinking

- **Standard / Premium models (Kling 3.0 etc.):** hero shots — faces, dialogue, key story beats.
- **Turbo / Lite models:** iteration, B-roll, establishers, tests. Draft cheap, render the winners expensive.
- **One clip at a time, quality-gated:** a failed clip never chains. Re-prompt, don't hope.

## Reliability rules

1. Never spend credits on a guess — pre-check the prompt against the checklists in `prompt-engineering.md`.
2. Failed/NSFW generations aren't billed on the API path; verify billing behavior in the app before a big batch.
3. Credits reset each billing cycle and don't roll over — plan usage so paid credits don't evaporate.
4. Higgsfield open-sourced three of its own AI films with every prompt, camera setting, and asset published — mine those before inventing your own pipeline.

## Sources
- https://higgsfield.ai/creator-hub/help-center/ai-models/how-do-i-create-and-use-a-soul-id-character
- https://www.thehypemagazine.com/2026/10/09/what-is-higgsfield-ai-uses-features-pricing/

<!-- chapter: higgsfield/prompt-engineering.md -->
# Higgsfield Prompt Engineering

## The anatomy of a prompt that works

Treat the prompt as a directing system, not a description. Every generation should specify, in order:

1. **Subject** — who/what, locked identity
2. **Micro-action** — one believable action, not three
3. **Environment** — where, with subtle motion in it
4. **Camera behavior** — one intentional move (see below)
5. **Lighting design** — explicit and physical ("golden-hour side light, long shadows")
6. **Visual style** — cinematic, anamorphic, film grain, era
7. **Emotional tone** — the feeling of the shot
8. **Physics & motion details** — how things move (cloth in breeze, steam rising)
9. **Rendering quality modifiers** — 4K, shallow depth of field, stable architecture

Missing layers = randomness. "Slow dolly push-in" beats "zoom in." Explicit lighting beats "nice lighting."

## Camera phrasing that the models obey

- **Push-in / reveal:** "the camera slowly dollies toward the subject with smooth stabilized movement"
- **Pull-back / scale:** "the camera slowly pulls backward, gradually revealing the enormous environment surrounding the subject"
- **Orbit:** "camera orbits 360° around the subject"
- **Pan:** "slow camera pan across the scene"
- **Stacked moves:** Higgsfield's Cinema Studio supports several moves in one shot — but one motivated move beats two unmotivated ones.

Rule: every movement needs a purpose. Ask what the move reveals or withholds.

## The Soul ID prompting rule

When a Soul ID character is active, **do not re-describe the face or core features** — the Soul ID handles that. Describe only what changes: wardrobe, setting, action, expression, camera, light, style.

Good: "The Soul ID character now wears a formal black suit, standing at a podium addressing a conference room. Camera: dolly in toward her face. Style: cinematic, cool corporate lighting."

## The exclusion block

Always exclude what breaks cinematic output: morphing faces, extra limbs, melting hands, warping architecture, flicker, watermark-like artifacts, text in frame (unless wanted). Put it in every prompt, not just the risky ones.

## Per-shot discipline

- One shot = one fully self-contained prompt. Restate the full premise every time — the model has no memory of your last clip.
- Don't ask for too many actions in five seconds. One action per clip.
- Keep the frame uncrowded. Fewer subjects = fewer failure modes.
- Image-to-video (start frame first) beats text-to-video for control. Generate the still, approve it, then animate.

## Common failure modes and fixes

| Failure | Fix |
|---|---|
| Face morphs mid-shot | Shorter clip; Soul ID or reference image; re-generate from a locked start frame |
| Melting hands | Keep hands out of frame or still; exclude "deformed hands"; crop in post |
| Camera drift (unmotivated) | Pin an end frame; name one explicit camera move; shorten duration |
| Identity drift across shots | Soul ID; same seed discipline; approved-frame library as start frames |
| Flicker / texture boil | Regenerate; avoid overly busy backgrounds; stabilize in post |
| Plasticky faces in wide shots | Shoot closer; composite a close-shot face in post |

- https://higgsfield.ai/creator-hub/help-center/ai-models/how-do-i-create-and-use-a-soul-id-character

<!-- chapter: higgsfield/soul-id-deep-dive.md -->
# Soul ID Deep Dive

## What it is

Soul ID is Higgsfield's character-consistency layer: train it once on photos of one person and the same face appears across every generation — any style, pose, lighting, or angle. It's the equivalent of casting the same actor for the entire film.

A reference image anchors a single generation but drifts across many. Soul ID trains a reusable identity once and holds it.

## How to train (official requirements)

From Higgsfield's help center:

1. Open higgsfield.ai → **Soul** → **Train new character**
2. **Prepare photos:** 20 or more of the same person (up to 80 supported)
   - High-quality and well-lit
   - Face from different angles and expressions
   - No sunglasses, no heavy shadows, no cropped faces
   - Include at least one full-height photo
   - Recent photos for the most accurate likeness
   - Only your own face or someone who gave permission
3. Upload and start training — takes a few minutes
4. Name the character
5. Generate — select it in the **Character** tab

## Using it in production

- **Soul ID locks identity; everything else follows your prompt.** Wardrobe, setting, action, camera, light — all prompt-driven.
- **Prompting rule:** never re-describe the face. Describe only what changes from the base character.
- **Works across the Soul family** (Soul 2.0, Soul Cinema, Cinema Studio, Marketing Studio, supported video models).
- **Caveat:** Soul IDs are tied to the model they were trained in — a character trained in Soul 2.0 may need retraining for Soul Cinema. Verify before a big shoot.

## When to use it / when to skip it

Use: multi-shot sequences, short films with a recurring protagonist, series content, AI influencers, brand mascots, action sequences needing the same hero.

Skip: single one-off shots (overkill), or when you want maximum creative variation — consistency limits style range.

## Identity drift: causes and fixes

- **Drift across many generations:** re-anchor with the trained Soul ID selected; don't fall back to per-generation reference uploads.
- **Wide-shot face collapse:** faces go plasticky at distance — shoot closer, or composite a close-shot face in post.
- **Feature drift:** keep a character sheet (front, 3/4, side reference) and use it as the reference image when drift appears.
- **Never fabricate identity frames.** The trained Soul ID is the identity authority — every clip's face must trace back to it, never to an invented start frame.

## Sources
- https://higgsfield.ai/creator-hub/help-center/ai-models/how-do-i-create-and-use-a-soul-id-character
- https://www.thehypemagazine.com/2026/10/09/what-is-higgsfield-ai-uses-features-pricing/
- https://github.com/ianfr13/higgsfield-ai-prompt-skill/blob/HEAD/mnt/user-data/outputs/higgsfield/skills/higgsfield-soul/SKILL.md

<!-- chapter: higgsfield/competition-entry-craft.md -->
# Competition-entry craft

Judged AI-film competitions are a production teacher, not a lottery ticket. This chapter is about what their constraints and judging criteria teach you about making professional work — whether or not you ever enter one.

## Why competitions are worth studying

A competition hands you three things most productions never get:

1. **Hard constraints** — runtime limits, delivery specs, content rules. Constraints are a forcing function for craft: every decision the rules make for you is a decision you can't get wrong.
2. **A published quality bar** — judging criteria tell you exactly what experienced eyes score: directing, craft, sound, originality. That's a checklist you can aim any film at.
3. **A body of judged work** — winning entries are public. Shot-by-shot teardowns of what placed are the cheapest film school available (see `case-studies/competition-teardowns.md`).

## The constraint set that shapes production

Real competition rulebooks converge on the same production discipline. Treat each as a standing habit:

- **Runtime discipline.** Competitions cap entries at a few minutes. The craft lesson: a 3-minute film that lands beats a 10-minute film that drifts. Budget your runtime like your credits — every shot must earn its seconds.
- **Delivery specs are real.** Watermarks, packshots, aspect ratios, masters. The craft lesson: professional delivery is a package, not a file. Build your delivery checklist before you lock picture (see `skills/delivery/`).
- **Rights hygiene.** Competition rules typically require AI-generated music/voice/sound with rights held by the creator. The craft lesson: clear every asset's rights at generation time, not at delivery. Keep the receipts in your asset registry.
- **Likeness safety.** "No real person's face or voice" is a common rule — not even your own. The craft lesson: never build a film on likeness you can't clear. Synthetic characters and Soul IDs are the safe default.
- **Small teams, async.** Winning entries are routinely made by 2–4 people across time zones. The craft lesson: a tight team with a shared asset registry beats a large team with a group chat.

## What juries actually reward

Across Runway AIFF, Project Odyssey, Reply AIFF, the Higgsfield Action Contest, and MIT's hackathon, judges reward the same things: **story over spectacle, authorial intent, character/POV discipline, originality, sound design, and polish as the floor.** They punish: visible morphing/inconsistency, generic "AI slop," tech demos without narrative, and AI that pulls focus from the story.

Distilled: narrative cohesion + committed POV + intentional AI use + pro-grade sound + consistent visuals. Originality is the tiebreaker; polish is the entry ticket.

Direct for that jury — story, cinematography, craft — not for the AI-tools audience. The film that wins is the one that would work if nobody knew how it was made.

## Craft patterns from judged work

Higgsfield's Action Contest (8,752 submissions, 139 countries) shows what experienced filmmakers do with AI:

- **"GRANDMA vs WASP"** — Muhannad Nassar & Simon Meyer. The makers never met in person; fully async workflow across time zones. *Lesson:* decentralized production works when the asset pipeline is disciplined.
- **"CUPID"** — Shestak Nikolay, actor/filmmaker. Concepts that would need prohibitive traditional budgets. *Lesson:* AI used for impossible scale, not novelty.
- **"SCRATCH"** — Ash & Aram Gevorkyan, made in **five days**. Director + 3D/VFX generalist duo; production value audiences mistook for a studio trailer. *Lesson:* a tight team with real craft compresses schedules AI can't compress alone.

Pattern: experienced filmmakers using AI for impossible scale, tight teams, real craft — not tech demos.

## Study the open-sourced winners

Higgsfield open-sourced three of its own AI films with every prompt, camera setting, and asset published. Before spending a credit, study a complete production's actual prompts and settings — it's the closest thing to sitting in someone else's edit bay.

## Competition-entry delivery checklist

- [ ] Final cut locked to the runtime cap, master to spec (aspect, watermark/packshot if required)
- [ ] All music/voice/sound rights cleared and documented in the asset registry
- [ ] No uncleared likeness anywhere in the film
- [ ] Credits and key art treated as craft, not an afterthought
- [ ] Team roles and handoffs defined before production starts

## Sources
- https://higgsfield.ai/blog/higgsfield-global-film-festival
- https://aivideosensei.com/guides/higgsfield-global-film-festival-guide
- https://medium.com/@sanwsman7/i-didnt-believe-ai-could-make-a-real-film-until-i-tried-higgsfield-ai-de0b4ee68072
- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=babNcxpwnx0 (Action Contest winner reveal)
- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZoqzD_NMa4w ("CUPID")
<!-- chapter: craft/story-structure.md -->
# Story Structure for AI Short Films

## The short-film engine

A 3–5 minute AI film needs exactly three things:

1. **One want** — the protagonist wants something concrete, visible on screen
2. **One obstacle** — something specific stands in the way
3. **One turn** — the moment everything changes

Most AI-film losers are tech demos with no second act: pretty shots, no turn. Judges (especially Oscar-caliber ones) punish this first.

## The judged-short template

- **Cold open (0:00–0:30):** drop into the world mid-action. No setup, no title cards explaining the premise.
- **Escalation (0:30–2:30):** the want meets the obstacle, pressure builds. Each shot raises the stakes or deepens the world.
- **Reversal (2:30–3:30):** the turn — the plan fails, the truth lands, the choice gets made.
- **Button (3:30–5:00):** one final image that reframes everything before it. End on the image, not on explanation.

## Writing for the model

Design scenes around what AI renders well; write away from what it doesn't.

**Lean into:** single subjects, strong silhouettes, weather and atmosphere, landscapes, slow deliberate motion, objects and environments, stylized looks.

**Write around:** complex hand action, crowd choreography, intricate dialogue scenes, fast fight choreography, text/signage in frame, real people or voices (festival rules forbid them anyway).

**The constraint is the style:** the best AI films don't hide the medium — they pick stories the medium tells better than live action could (impossible scale, dream logic, metamorphosis).

## Scene design checklist (per scene)

- [ ] One clear want visible in the frame
- [ ] One action per shot, five seconds or less each
- [ ] The turn is a visual event, not dialogue
- [ ] Every scene either raises stakes or deepens world — never both vaguely, never neither
- [ ] The ending image is planned before the first shot is generated
<!-- chapter: craft/cinematic-language.md -->
# Cinematic Language

The shot vocabulary and camera grammar that make AI video read as cinema instead of a screensaver.

## Shot sizes — what each one is for

| Shot | Use |
|---|---|
| Extreme wide | World, scale, isolation |
| Wide | Geography — where the story happens |
| Medium | Action and dialogue — the workhorse |
| Close-up | Emotion, decision, detail |
| Extreme close-up | Texture, eyes, objects that matter |

Festival rule of thumb: earn your close-ups. Wide → medium → close builds pressure; starting close spends it.

## Camera movements — the working lexicon

| Move | Prompt phrasing | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Dolly in / push-in | "camera slowly dollies toward the subject, smooth stabilized movement" | Portraits, reveals, rising tension |
| Dolly out / pull-back | "camera pulls backward, revealing the environment around the subject" | Scale, aftermath, loneliness |
| Pan | "slow camera pan across the scene" | Surveys, transitions between subjects |
| Orbit | "camera orbits around the subject" | Hero moments, product, dance |
| Crane | "camera rises and pulls back, revealing the scene from above" | Endings, scope |
| Handheld | "subtle handheld shake, documentary feel" | Urgency, realism — use sparingly |
| Static | "locked-off static camera" | Dialogue, tension, confidence |

"Slow dolly push-in" beats "zoom in" every time — name the physical move, not the effect.

**Motivated vs unmotivated:** every move must reveal or withhold something. A drifting camera with no purpose is the #1 tell of amateur AI video. If you can't say why the camera moves, lock it off.

## Lighting — write it like a gaffer

Vague lighting gets vague images. Specify direction, quality, and color:

- **Direction:** side light, backlight/rim, top light, underlight
- **Quality:** hard noon sun, soft overcast, flickering torchlight, neon spill
- **Color/temperature:** golden-hour warmth, cold blue night, sodium-orange street
- **Motivation:** every light needs a source in the world — window, lamp, neon sign

Example: "dramatic golden-hour side lighting with long shadows" will always beat "nice lighting."

## Composition

- **Rule of thirds:** place the subject off-center; give the frame somewhere to breathe
- **Depth staging:** foreground, midground, background all doing something — this is what makes AI shots feel expensive
- **Leading lines:** roads, corridors, light beams pulling the eye to the subject
- **Negative space:** emptiness is a compositional choice — isolation, scale, dread
- **Don't overcrowd:** fewer subjects per frame = fewer failure modes

## The "cinematic" recipe

"Cinematic" is not a word you add — it's five things combined:

1. **Camera** — one intentional movement
2. **Subject** — one believable action
3. **Environment** — subtle motion (dust, smoke, cloth, water)
4. **Lighting** — explicit, motivated, consistent
5. **Texture** — film grain, anamorphic cues, shallow depth of field

Example: "Slow cinematic dolly forward toward an ancient temple entrance. Priests walk calmly up stone steps while torch flames flicker. Thin smoke rises into warm evening air. Cloth banners move gently in the breeze. Stable architecture, realistic human motion, dramatic golden-hour lighting."

Note: every movement has a purpose, and the prompt asks for exactly one action per subject.

- https://github.com/servanter/ai-magic/blob/HEAD/content/blog/best-ai-video-generators-2026-sora-runway-kling-pika-comparison.mdx
- https://medium.com/@gencaycubuk/i-tested-dozens-of-runway-prompts-this-framework-creates-cinematic-ai-videos-every-time-e171658033e1

<!-- chapter: craft/character-consistency.md -->
# Character Consistency

The technical discipline of keeping people and worlds stable across shots. This is where most festival entries die.

## The identity stack (ranked by reliability)

1. **Trained identity (Soul ID):** the gold standard. Train once on 20–80 photos; the face holds across every generation. See `higgsfield/soul-id-deep-dive.md`.
2. **Character sheet as reference:** front / 3/4 / side views of the character, used as the reference image whenever drift appears.
3. **Per-generation reference upload:** anchors one generation; drifts across many. Fine for single shots, not films.
4. **Text description alone:** weakest. Never rely on prose to hold a face across 50 shots.

## Wardrobe and props lock

- Write the wardrobe once, in exact language, and paste it verbatim into every prompt: "worn brown leather jacket, white t-shirt, dark jeans, scuffed boots."
- Props get the same treatment: one description, reused exactly.
- If the wardrobe changes mid-film (it should, for story), that's a new locked description — never improvise it per shot.

## World consistency

- **Locations:** generate and approve a master still of each location first. Every shot in that location starts from it or references it.
- **Lighting continuity:** lock time of day and light direction per scene. "Golden-hour side light from frame left" in every prompt of the scene.
- **Era/grade:** pick the era and color palette up front (Higgsfield's era selection helps); don't grade shot-by-shot and hope.

## The chaining discipline

- **Last-frame chaining:** every clip starts from the last frame of the previous approved clip. Never fabricate a start frame.
- **Approved-frame library:** keep every approved still/frame. New shots start from library frames, not fresh generations.
- **Rejection rules:** a clip fails if the face drifts, wardrobe changes, the light flips, or the camera moves without motivation. Failed clips don't chain — they get re-prompted.
- **One human per start frame** (for character-led work): crowded frames multiply failure modes.

## The consistency checklist (before any generation)

- [ ] Identity system chosen and trained (Soul ID for films)
- [ ] Wardrobe description locked, verbatim
- [ ] Location master stills approved
- [ ] Light direction + time of day locked per scene
- [ ] Start frame is real (approved frame or trained identity), never invented
<!-- chapter: craft/directing-performance.md -->
# Directing Performance in AI Video

AI models don't act. They render plausible arrangements of pixels that read as acting when the direction is specific enough — and collapse into mannequin theater when it isn't. This chapter is the directing discipline behind believable AI performance, drawn from productions that solved it in public.

## The core problem

Passport Rush's team documented it openly: **AI struggles with subtle character acting.** The failure has a shape:

- Faces average toward neutral — micro-expressions collapse into a pleasant blank
- Emotion labels ("she looks devastated") produce stock expressions, not felt ones
- Dead, glassy eyes — the single fastest tell of an undirected AI performance
- The Verge's review of Cully Hill Boys noted "occasionally weak character interactions" as a visible limit even at $2M

The fix is not a better model. It's direction written the way actors need it — as *tasks*, not adjectives.

## Direct, don't describe

ONEIRIC's acting skill (`tig-acting-task`) replaced emotion labels with acting tasks entirely. The closing rule of that production: **direct, don't describe** — scene event, motive, goal, obstacle, tactic.

| Instead of (description) | Write (direction) |
|---|---|
| She looks devastated | She is trying not to cry in front of him — jaw set, eyes on the door |
| He is furious | He is deciding whether to hit him — weight shifting forward, hands opening and closing |
| They are in love | She keeps finding reasons to stand closer; he keeps noticing and not moving away |
| He is nervous | He is rehearsing what to say — lips moving silently, thumb rubbing the ring |

Every entry on the right is a *playable tactic* — something a body can do. Models can't render "devastated." They can render a jaw set and eyes fixed on a door.

## Give the eyes a job

The single highest-leverage performance note in the research: **"dead, glassy eyes are never fixed with lighting — they're fixed by giving the eyes a job."**

The CINEDANCE prompt architecture gives GAZE/EYELINES its own block *before* blocking. In practice:

- Name the eyeline target per beat: *Mara holds on Vex's hands until "the ledger" — then snaps to his eyes*
- Eyes move between targets; they never "look sad into the middle distance"
- Avert, hold, search, track — eye verbs are direction, not decoration
- In dialogue coverage, the listener's eyes do half the acting — cut to the listener

If a performance feels dead, check the eyes first. Nine times out of ten there's no eyeline written.

## One feeling per shot

AI can't play an arc inside a single clip. It can hold one tactic for 4–8 seconds. So:

- Break emotional turns into separate shots — the turn happens *in the cut*
- The reaction shot is your best friend: AI renders listening better than it renders complex feeling
- Moment-to-moment tactics tied to dialogue words (the `tig-acting-task` block form): each line gets its own tactic, each tactic its own shot if needed

## The director's read

Before generating a scene, ONEIRIC's pipeline produced a "director's read": **the one shared event every character lives through, plus each character's physical channel for it.** Everyone in the scene is experiencing the same event — but grief lives in Mara's hands, in Vex's jaw, in the kid's feet. Write the event once, then assign each character their channel. This is what keeps ensemble scenes from becoming four mannequins emoting at the camera.

## Casting the face

Consistent identity *reads* as good acting. A face that drifts 5% between shots reads as a bad performance even when the "acting" is fine:

- Lock the face anchor; never re-run the base portrait
- State changes (dirt, wounds, tears) are masked integrations, not re-generations
- For recurring characters, identity systems (Soul ID and equivalents) beat per-prompt description

The audience forgives a limited performance from a consistent face. It never forgives a great "take" from a stranger.

## Ration the close-up

Micro-acting is the weakest link in every current model. Spend close-ups at emotional peaks — that's where the audience looks hardest and where the model fails most visibly. Wides and mediums carry the rest; they read as confident filmmaking anyway.

## Dialogue performance

- Short lines per generation; native-audio quotes for the delivery, not the face
- Let the voice carry the acting — don't ask the face to do what the voice already does
- The listener's reaction shot sells the line more than the speaker's mouth
- For long scenes: generate silent, isolate vocals, post lip-sync — the performance lives in the edit

## Rehearsal is drafts

Treat 720p drafts as rehearsal takes. Watch for: does the tactic read? Do the eyes have a job? Does the turn land in the cut? Re-direct with changed variables — a new tactic, a new eyeline — never the same prompt hoping. Three failed rehearsals means simplify the shot, not the actor.

## When to go hybrid

Some performances AI can't give you yet. The documented answer: put a real human at the emotional core and let AI handle everything around them.

- **Get Me Out**: a real performer captured the emotion; AI re-skinned the world around her
- **Dreams of Violets**: the director voice-acted every role himself, then AI-converted each character's voice — the performance was human, the timbre was synthetic
- **Cully Hill Boys**: licensed likenesses with expressions and kinematics mapped from the performers' own photos and voice audio — the "acting" was anchored in real performers from the start

Rule of thumb: if the scene's entire job is one human feeling something complicated, that's the scene to shoot for real — or to voice for real — and transform with AI.

## The performance checklist

- [ ] Every emotional beat rewritten as a playable tactic
- [ ] Eyelines named per beat — every pair of eyes has a job
- [ ] One tactic per shot; turns happen in the cut
- [ ] Director's read written: shared event + each character's physical channel
- [ ] Close-ups rationed to emotional peaks
- [ ] Identity locked — no drift between "takes"
- [ ] Dialogue: voice carries, face supports, listener sells
- [ ] Drafts reviewed as rehearsals, re-directed with changed variables
- [ ] The emotional core scenes assessed honestly: AI or hybrid?

## Sources

- ONEIRIC production brief: `tig-acting-task` skill, CINEDANCE block order, closing rules (via community transcription of the open-sourced brief — flagged as third-party)
- Passport Rush breakdown: documented subtle-acting problem (official YouTube breakdown)
- Cully Hill Boys: licensed likeness pipeline, expressions/kinematics from performer reference (cryptobriefing.com, archyde.com)
- The Verge on Cully Hill Boys: "occasionally weak character interactions" (via magazine.mindplex.ai summary)
- Companion: `craft/character-consistency.md`, `craft/long-form-pipeline.md`, skills `craft-gaze-eyelines`, `audio-direct-voiceover`
<!-- chapter: craft/color-grading.md -->
# Color Grading AI Footage

Every AI generation arrives with its own built-in grade — the model's idea of what "cinematic" looks like, baked into the pixels. On a multi-shot production, that's 40 different colorists who never met. The colorist's job on AI footage is **unification**: bringing neighboring shots to one look.

## The two places color lives

**In the plate (before generation).** Lens character, palette direction, texture, time-of-day — baked into the location/character image plates. What you bake, you don't have to fix. The ONEIRIC rule: *the plate itself becomes the lens.*

**In the grade (after generation).** Shot-to-shot matching, the show look, technical delivery. What the plate couldn't hold.

Decide per element which place it lives. Anything the video model keeps dropping belongs in the plate. Anything that needs to move across the whole film belongs in the grade.

## The unification pass

Before any creative grading, unify. Pick one hero shot per scene as the reference. For every other shot:

1. Match exposure and white balance to the reference (scopes, not eyes)
2. Match contrast curve — AI generations vary wildly in black level
3. Match saturation — see the de-plasticize stack below
4. Only then apply the creative look

Do the unification pass over the location set *before* generating where possible (the ADILIADA production did this) — it's cheaper than discovering mismatch in the grade.

## The de-plasticize stack

AI footage has a recognizable syndrome: over-smooth gradients, over-saturated color, waxy skin, a sheen over everything. The fix, in order:

1. **Desaturate 10–20%.** AI oversaturates by default. This one move does half the work.
2. **Add fine film grain.** 35mm grain breaks up the smooth gradients that scream synthetic. Grain is the fastest anti-plastic pass in existence.
3. **Subtle chromatic aberration** at high-contrast edges. Real lenses have flaws; perfect edges read as rendered.
4. **Soften, don't sharpen.** Plastic + sharp = worse. A whisper of diffusion beats any sharpening pass.
5. **Skin last.** Skin is the hardest surface — if it's waxy, a dedicated skin-refinement pass or slight diffusion on skin tones only.

Check the whole stack on a big screen. Defects invisible on a laptop appear at 4K.

## Matching across models

Different models have different "house grades" — Kling's contrast curve isn't Veo's. When a scene mixes models:

- Unify harder: match to the reference before any creative look
- The plate matters more: shared plates across models do more than any grade can
- If two models won't match, re-generate the outlier rather than torturing the grade

## The show look

Once unified, the creative grade. For AI film, restraint wins:

- One look for the film, with scene-level variations — not a new look per scene
- Work in passes: primary (whole image) → secondaries (skin, sky, key objects) → texture (grain, halation, gate weave if period)
- Halation and bloom flatter AI highlights, which tend to clip harshly
- Decide the grain philosophy early: one grain for the film, applied at the end, over everything — it's the final unifier

## Scopes, not eyes

Grade with waveforms and vectorscopes. AI footage lies to eyes — the "cinematic" built-in grade is designed to flatter on first glance. Check:

- Blacks actually reach black (AI loves milky shadows)
- Skin tones sit on the skin-tone line (vectorscope)
- Saturation doesn't clip in any channel

## Delivery

- Festival masters: 16:9 or 21:9 composed (not cropped) for the ratio, up to 4K
- Broadcast-safe levels; -1 dBTP audio ceiling is the sound department's job, but don't crush the picture to compensate
- Keep the pre-grade masters. When the festival asks for a revision, you re-grade — you don't re-generate.

## The grading checklist

- [ ] Look decided per element: plate vs grade
- [ ] Unification pass before creative grading (reference still per scene)
- [ ] De-plasticize stack applied: desat, grain, CA, soften
- [ ] Skin checked on a big screen
- [ ] Multi-model scenes matched or re-generated
- [ ] One show look, scene variations — not a look per scene
- [ ] Scopes verify blacks, skin line, saturation
- [ ] Pre-grade masters archived

## Sources

- ONEIRIC brief: colorist-as-unification, bake-the-look-into-plates (third-party transcription — flagged)
- ADILIADA: pre-generation unification pass over the location set
- Companion: skills `craft-kill-ai-look`, `fix-plasticky-look`, `craft-bake-look`
<!-- chapter: craft/sound-music-audio.md -->
# Sound, Music & Audio

Sound is half the picture. Amateur AI films are silent; winners are designed. (Festival rules require AI-generated music, voice, and sound — this isn't optional.)

## Native audio

Some video models generate audio natively with the clip. Rules:

- **Keep it when** it's ambient texture: room tone, wind, rain, crowd murmur, footsteps.
- **Strip it when** it's dialogue, music, or anything prominent — regenerate those deliberately.
- **Never** let native audio be your only sound layer. It's a bed, not a mix.

## Sound design (the layer that sells reality)

Every scene needs three layers:

1. **Bed:** ambient tone of the location (room, street, forest, wind) — runs under everything.
2. **Foley:** footsteps, cloth, object handling — the sounds that make movement feel physical.
3. **Accents:** designed hits for story beats — the turn, the reveal, the button.

AI SFX tools can generate all three from text prompts. Describe sounds the way you describe shots: specifically and physically.

## Score

- AI music generators take prompts like: "ambient synth, 85 BPM, rising tension, no vocals."
- **Temp-track discipline:** cut to a temp score first, then generate the final score to the locked cut — never score to a moving target.
- No vocals unless the story needs them; score serves the story, never shows off.
- The festival requires AI-generated music with rights you hold — keep the generation receipts.

## Dialogue

- **When AI dialogue works:** short lines, clean delivery, minimal background noise in the reference audio.
- **When it doesn't:** long speeches, overlapping voices, emotional extremes. Write around these — visual storytelling over talk.
- **Lip-sync pipeline:** generate the visual first, then sync: feed clean WAV audio into the platform's lip-sync (Pika and Runway both offer it; clean audio in = believable sync out).
- **Rule:** if the line doesn't change the story, cut it. Festival shorts win on images.

## The audio checklist

- [ ] Ambient bed under every scene
- [ ] Foley on all physical movement
- [ ] Score generated to the locked cut
- [ ] Dialogue minimal, clean, synced
- [ ] Final mix: dialogue > score > bed (nothing fights the story)
- [ ] All audio AI-generated with rights documented (festival requirement)
<!-- chapter: craft/editing-pipeline.md -->
# Editing Pipeline

From selects to festival-ready export.

## Assembly

- **Selects discipline:** generate 2–4 takes per shot, keep the best one. Kill darlings — a beautiful shot that doesn't serve the story is a deleted shot.
- **Cut to the story, not the footage:** the shot list is a plan, not a prison. If a generated shot is better than planned, re-cut around it.
- **Keep ratios honest:** 45–75 shots for a 3–5 minute film. Fewer, better shots beat more, weaker ones.

## Transitions and pacing

- **Cuts over effects.** Hard cuts are invisible; dissolves and wipes announce themselves. Use transitions only when time or place changes.
- **Pacing math:** action sequences cut faster (1–2s shots), emotional beats breathe (4–6s). Vary rhythm deliberately — monotony is the enemy.
- **The J-cut/L-cut:** let audio lead or lag the picture cut. Instant professionalism, costs nothing.

## Color

- **Match AI shots to each other first:** different models and prompts produce different grades. Normalize before styling.
- **One LUT direction for the whole film:** pick the palette in pre-production (era selection helps) and apply consistently.
- **The "expensive" grade:** restrained contrast, skin tones natural, shadows with detail. Over-saturated teal-and-orange reads cheap.
- **Free tools:** CapCut handles LUTs, grain, contrast, and saturation well enough for festival delivery.

## VFX touch-up

- **Cleanup passes:** inpaint glitches, stabilize micro-jitter, remove stray artifacts.
- **Face composite:** plasticky wide-shot faces get replaced with crops from close-shot frames.
- **Grain:** a light film-grain overlay unifies shots from different models — the cheapest consistency tool in post.
- **Upscale last:** finish the edit, then upscale the final timeline — never upscale individual clips and re-edit.

## Delivery

- **Export specs:** match the festival's required format, resolution, and codec exactly.
- **Watermark + packshot:** the Higgsfield festival requires both in the final video — build them into the export, not as an afterthought.
- **Watch it on three screens:** phone, laptop, TV. If it only looks good on one, the grade isn't done.
- **The 24-hour rule:** lock the cut, sleep, watch fresh. Every flaw you catch now is one the jury won't.

## The delivery checklist

- [ ] Picture lock before color and mix
- [ ] Color matched across all shots, one palette
- [ ] Sound mix final (dialogue > score > bed)
- [ ] VFX cleanup pass complete
- [ ] Watermark + packshot embedded
- [ ] Exported to festival spec
- [ ] Watched fresh on multiple screens
<!-- chapter: craft/long-form-pipeline.md -->
# The Long-Form Pipeline: Making AI Films at 20+ Minutes

Short films are won with great prompts. Long films are won with *systems*. Everything in this chapter comes from productions that actually shipped long-form AI work — most of it open-sourced by Higgsfield — and every number carries its source. Where the research couldn't verify something, it's flagged.

## The core insight

Across every documented long-form AI production, the through-line is the same: **assets before shots, always.** Locked character sheets, locations, and props exist as named, versioned records *before* any video is generated. The working shape is:

- `brief.md` — logline, tools, pre/prod/post plan
- `script.md` — the screenplay
- `registry.md` — the constants: named looks per world, one verbatim descriptor per @-tagged asset
- one `shotlist.md` per scene — each shot: number, seconds, one-line goal, the **entire prompt verbatim**, `look:`, optional `source:`
- `log.md` — version history per shot: version, what changed, takes, verdict

Cully Hill Boys published a **137-entry version log**. ONEIRIC generated **41,118 assets for ~20 minutes**. The scale of waste — not the cost per clip — is the real budget line.

## Case snapshots

### The Cully Hill Boys — 110 min, ~$2M, 4 weeks, 28 people

The first fully AI-generated feature with licensed celebrity likenesses (Israel Adesanya, Quinton "Rampage" Jackson, streamer N3on, Matt "MK" Kiatipis). Seedance 2.5 for video + speech, Claude for prompt crafting, Seedream and Nano Banana for polish. ~1,000 production-ready assets across ~100 locations in 4K. About half the budget (~$1M) went to compute; the rest covered likeness licensing, creative direction, screenplay, and finishing. Forty percent of the crew had no prior AI experience — the roles were directorial and editorial, not ML.

Key mechanics:
- Character sheets built from the licensed talents' photos and audio, locking face, body, clothing, and voice *before* generation began. Talent supplied ~2 minutes of voice audio; biometrics were contractually purged within 30 days.
- A shared canvas system held sheets, locations, props, and state so parallel teams stayed in continuity.
- Average prompt: **over 3,000 words with 10+ image references per scene** (per Higgsfield co-founder Alex Mashrabov).
- Open-sourced: prompts, production logs, workflow docs, character cards, raw assets — via Higgsfield Academy and YouTube.

### ONEIRIC — 20 min, made for Higgsfield's film competition

**Correction:** earlier versions of this guide described a Cannes premiere for ONEIRIC. The research found no source connecting it to Cannes — its official description says it was made on Cinema Studio 4 *for the Higgsfield Global Film Festival*. The Cannes-adjacent AI screening was *Hell Grind's*, and that was a third-party industry showcase, not an official selection.

Four friends, four genres (Troy battle, galactic cruiser chase, griffin flight, dorm-room drama). Open-sourced: every Seedance asset and prompt, plus Claude skills for scripting (`tig-scene-engine`), acting direction (`tig-acting-task`), and shot prompting (`tig-diagram`).

Key mechanics:
- **The blocking diagram:** when a shot needs precise multi-character staging, words stop working. A color-coded schematic outline is attached *last* among references so photos win the style vote; the prompt binds each color to a character tag. Rules: front view from the camera's side (never a top-down plan — "video models think in frames, not blueprints"), letters live in prompt text only, edits address colors not characters ("move the BLUE figure").
- **The consistent-lens-look trick:** asking for an anamorphic look in the video prompt fails — optics drift shot to shot. Fix: bake the optics into the *location image* plate. **The plate itself becomes the lens.**
- **Two-pass character sheets:** Soul Cinema makes the face in close-up (the identity anchor); Soul 2.0 builds full-body looks from it. Hard rule: **the base portrait is never re-run through any model** — variants are integrated with masks around the base pixels. Re-running a portrait is how a character "slowly stops being the same person."
- **State = new asset:** `@char_ON_Rudy_s2_v1` — character + project + scene + version. A state change gets a new tag, never an overwrite.
- **Voice Bible pasted verbatim** into every generation — not even a synonym changed.
- **Every prompt is an island:** positions, poses, wardrobe, props, optics, light spelled out from scratch every time. "Same as the previous shot" is an instruction to a model with no "before."
- Post ran five stages: assembly → rough cut → **generation supervision** (a scheduled QC/re-generation pass *after* the rough cut, not continuous re-rolling) → fine cut with cold viewers → picture lock.

### Passport Rush — hybrid, 18 scenes in 3 days

Hand-drawn 2D storyboards → Soul 2.0 character sheets → Photoshop hand-painted fixes → **Blender previz** (camera, action timing, squash-and-stretch; renders served as video references) → Claude Opus 5.5 scene prompts → Seedance 2.5. "Not a prompt. Not a model. A person with a pencil" — the boards locked story before any generation. The team documented their failures openly, including the subtle-acting problem: AI struggles with nuanced performance.

### Hell Grind — 95 min, 15 people, 14 days, <$500K

Seedance 2.0 via Cinema Studio (~33 aggregated models). **16,000+ clips generated → 253 final shots** (reported for the first episode — the film may be episodic, so don't quote it as a whole-film ratio). ~80% of budget on compute. Prompts averaged ~3,000 words for ~15 seconds of footage (single tabloid-grade source — flagged).

### Dreams of Violets — 75 min, Tribeca official selection

The counter-example to the big-budget approach: director Ash Koosha claims **$2,000 total GPU spend** (his own unaudited figure), covering "8–10 traditional jobs" himself — 786 videos cut in Resolve, ~1,000 audio clips, 35 minutes of original music, and he voice-acted every role himself at a London studio, then AI-converted each character's voice. First fully AI-generated feature in official programming at a major festival.

## The pipeline, step by step

### 1. Script first, then stress-test it

Every scene runs a Goal/Obstacle/Tactic/Reversal/Value-Shift verdict *before* generation — because a weak scene's cost is only discovered after you've generated it. Then a step-by-step storyboard: "only on the storyboard does it become clear how good a scene really is, as opposed to how good it was in your head."

### 2. Build the asset registry

One @-tag per asset, used everywhere. Character sheets (face close-up → full body), locations (with look baked in), props. Descriptors and fixed look/camera blocks live as constants so one edit updates every shot. The registry is the database.

### 3. Draw the blocking

For any multi-character staging: color-coded diagram, attached last, front camera view, edits by color. Add a depth map (black-and-white geometry channel) for room-heavy scenes — without it, "a location that rearranges itself every few seconds." Plant visual anchors (a specific chair, a window) that repeat across generations. Run a unification pass over the location set (color/light/saturation) *before* generating — cheaper than discovering mismatch in the grade.

### 4. Write island prompts

CINEDANCE block order: SCENE CONTEXT · ACTIVE REFERENCES · LOCATION MAP · GAZE/EYELINES · FIRST FRAME AND BLOCKING · SEGMENTS (timed beats) · DIALOGUE · AUDIO · PHYSICS · LIGHTING · STYLE/FORMAT · POSITIVE LOCKS. Gaze/eyelines get their own block before blocking; dialogue and audio are separated (audio carries voice identity only). Negatives policy: say what you want, not what you avoid — bans live at the image stage only, never in video prompts, and renderable nouns are never written even as negations.

### 5. Generate with a re-anchoring cadence

Chain each scene off the previous scene's *finished video* as reference — "a text description drifts over generations; a video reference doesn't." Schedule regeneration as a fixed pass after the rough cut, not a standing reaction. Budget continuity work on ordinary rooms, not spectacle: the research is explicit that a one-room dialogue scene held across dozens of shots was the hardest technical task of ONEIRIC — harder than the space battle.

### 6. Post like a film

Assembly → rough cut → generation supervision → fine cut → picture lock (no new generations except emergencies, with notice to color and sound). The colorist's job is **unification** — every generation ships its own built-in grade. Sound: dialogue generated natively with video where possible, or recorded human then AI-converted character by character.

## Compute budgeting (October 2026 retail rates)

Assumptions labeled: Seedance 2.5 API from ~$0.0738/s. A "clean pass" means every second generated exactly once — fiction in practice; the documented regime is 5–20× regeneration overhead.

| Film | Clean pass | Realistic envelope (5–20× overhead) |
|---|---|---|
| 20 min (1,200 s) | ~$89 | ~$500–$8,000 depending on resolution |
| 90 min (5,400 s) | ~$400 | ~$2,000–$40,000 at retail |

Why the company productions cost 100× that: Hell Grind's ~80% of $500K and Cully's ~$1M compute are *internal* infra costs at mid-2026 rates — plus licensed talent, 25–28-person teams, 4K, and heavy parallel overshoot. Do not quote the $1M figure as a retail budget; rates have already fallen since.

Sanity anchors: Koosha's claimed $2,000 GPU for 75 minutes (unaudited, with proprietary tooling); single-source reporting of $1,000–$3,000 for 20–30-minute microdramas (flagged).

## Team roles for a small AI feature crew

Observed across productions, not prescribed: writer, director(s), asset/continuity manager, prompt writer, editor, color, sound/music. Cully ran 28 with nine directors under two leads; Hell Grind ran 15 pros (directors, DPs, editors); Arena Zero's pilot ran on 4 people and 5,000+ generations; Koosha effectively ran solo. Recurring truth: 40% of Cully's crew had never used AI — the jobs are directorial and editorial.

## Failure modes unique to long-form

- **Drift accumulation** — identity and style decay across scenes. Counter: never re-run the base portrait; state = new asset; video-reference chaining.
- **Style decay** — optics/grade wandering per shot. Counter: bake the look into plates.
- **Blocked-position flips** — screen sides mirror, backgrounds swap. Counter: the color-coded diagram.
- **Memory-less prompting** — "same as the previous shot" silently fails. Counter: every prompt an island.
- **Summoning by negation** — banned words appear anyway. Counter: never write renderable nouns, even as bans.
- **Reference beats prompt** — a daylight kitchen reference overrules an evening prompt. Counter: put what you want in the reference.
- **Budget blowouts** — weak scenes discovered only after generation. Counter: stress-test first, scheduled regeneration passes.
- **The ordinary-scene cost trap** — one-room dialogue costs more than spectacle. Plan the re-roll budget accordingly.
- **The subtle-acting ceiling** — AI struggles with nuanced performance; write acting as eye-work and tactics, never emotion labels.

## What to steal — the long-form checklist

- [ ] Asset registry complete before shot one: every character, location, prop named, versioned, locked
- [ ] Every scene stress-tested (Goal/Obstacle/Tactic/Reversal/Value Shift) and storyboarded
- [ ] Blocking diagrams + depth maps for multi-character and room-heavy scenes
- [ ] Base portraits locked and never re-run; state changes = new tagged assets
- [ ] Look baked into plates; video prompts carry only what changes
- [ ] Voice Bible pasted verbatim into every generation
- [ ] Island prompts: everything re-stated, every time
- [ ] Video-reference chaining scene to scene
- [ ] 720p drafts; upscale winners only
- [ ] Generation supervision as a scheduled post-rough-cut pass
- [ ] Compute budget with 5–20× overhead, not the clean-pass number
- [ ] Picture lock means no new generations without notice to color and sound

- ONEIRIC: official YouTube description (verified live fetch — no Cannes mention); project brief via github.com/turapins/svvera (third-party transcription — flagged); Mashrabov LinkedIn announcement; higgsfield.ai/academy

<!-- chapter: platforms/field-guide.md -->
# AI Video Platform Field Guide

Every major platform, honestly assessed. Strengths, weaknesses, costs, and what each is actually best at.

## The field

| Platform | Signature strength | Weakness | Cost signal | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Higgsfield** | All-in-one: many engines, Soul ID, Cinema Studio presets, camera moves | Preset UI hides raw controls; shared credit pool obscures per-model price | Basic 120 / Pro 600 / Max 1,800 credits/mo; tiers Free–Premium (10+ credits) | Filmmaking workflow, character-led series |
| **Kling** (direct) | Photoreal physics (water, fire, smoke); end-frame pinning; multi-reference `elements` | Prompt engineering required, no hand-holding | ~0.6 units/sec 720p standard (~$0.084/sec); 0.8 pro; 3.0 native 4K | Hero shots when you want raw control |
| **Runway** (Gen-3/Gen-4) | Reference-image start + Motion Brush for exact motion control; human-centric scenes | Weaker without a strong start image | Paid tiers, full commercial rights | Ads, human scenes, precise motion |
| **Sora** | Epic scale, spectacle, narrative interpretation (prompts as mini-screenplays) | Access/cost; less steerable moment-to-moment | Premium tier | Vast scenes, ambitious concepts |
| **Luma Dream Machine** | Cinematic experimentation, smooth motion | Consistency weaker than leaders | Varies | Dreamlike / experimental passages |
| **Pika** | Lip-sync, character animation, playful effects; most permissive creatively | Less "cinematic" out of the box | Subscription | Dialogue, social, stylized work |
| **Hailuo / MiniMax** | VFX and fluid motion | Prompt nuance | Mid tier | Action, fluid dynamics |
| **Veo** | Nature/landscapes, reference-image fidelity, long coherent passages | Premium cost | Premium tier | Landscapes, documentary feel |
| **Wan** | Artistic / stylized video | Less photoreal | Mid tier | Stylized sequences |
| **Seedance** | Fast iteration speed | Top-end polish trails Kling/Sora | Mid tier | Drafting, volume work |

## Platform-specific prompting notes

- **Sora:** write prompts like mini-screenplays — scene direction, character actions, environment in sequential order.
- **Runway:** start with a strong reference image, then Motion Brush for movement. More predictable than text-only.
- **Kling:** keep prompts concise and direct; elaborate prose underperforms. Use motion templates.
- **Pika:** stack creative effects; for lip-sync feed clean audio with minimal background noise.

## Ownership and rights (verify before commercial use)

- Sora: users own generations (Opt-out of training data use on Enterprise).
- Runway: full commercial rights on paid tiers.
- Kling: commercial rights on Pro and above.
- Pika: full ownership on paid tiers; free tier restricts commercial use.

## The honest take

No single platform wins every shot. Festival-grade films are hybrid: pick the engine per shot, match color in post, and nobody will know. See `when-to-use-what.md`.

## Sources
- https://github.com/servanter/ai-magic/blob/HEAD/content/blog/best-ai-video-generators-2026-sora-runway-kling-pika-comparison.mdx
- https://www.meltflexai.com/blog/higgsfield-alternatives
- https://dyerbolical.com/mastering-ai-video-generation-in-2026-runway-pika-and-kling-for-professional-ads/
- https://github.com/ivan-meer/higgsfield-ai-prompt-skill/blob/HEAD/skills/higgsfield-models/SKILL.md
<!-- chapter: platforms/when-to-use-what.md -->
# When to Use What

The decision tree for picking the right tool per shot. Festival-grade films are hybrid — nobody will know if you match color in post.

## Decision rules

| Shot need | Reach for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Character close-up / dialogue | Higgsfield + Soul ID (Kling 3.0 engine) | Identity lock + top-tier faces + native audio |
| Epic scale / impossible environments | Sora 2 | Best vast-scene coherence |
| Nature / landscapes | Veo 3.1 | Reference-image fidelity, natural texture |
| Precise motion control | Runway + Motion Brush | Paint exactly where movement happens |
| Fast action / fluid VFX | Hailuo 2.3 | Fluid dynamics strength |
| Stylized / artistic passages | Wan 2.6 | Style over photorealism |
| Lip-sync dialogue | Pika | Clean-audio-in, synced lips out |
| Drafting / volume / tests | Seedance 2.0 Pro or Kling 2.5 Turbo | Speed and cost |
| Budget hero on a budget | Kling direct (end-frame pinning, elements) | Raw control without preset markup |

## The hybrid pipeline

1. **Plan per shot, not per film.** The shot list gets a model assignment column.
2. **Anchor on one identity system** (Soul ID) so faces survive platform-hopping.
3. **Generate in passes:** all drafts on cheap/fast models → approve → heroes on premium.
4. **Normalize in post:** one color pipeline, one grain overlay, one audio mix. This is what makes mixed sources invisible.
5. **Never switch models mid-scene** unless you have to — consistency is cheaper than correction.

## Cost-aware ordering

- Rough out the whole film on Turbo/Lite first (cheap).
- Identify the 10–15 hero shots that carry the story.
- Spend premium credits only on heroes and dialogue.
- Everything else ships from the draft pass with a good grade.

## Anti-patterns

- Using one platform for everything out of loyalty — you pay in quality somewhere.
- Premium-rendering a shot before the edit is locked — re-edits waste the expensive generation.
- Mixing aspect ratios across shots — pick delivery format on day one.
<!-- chapter: economics/credit-math.md -->
# Credit Math

Professional quality without burning the budget. The standing rule: **never spend credits on a guess.**

## What things cost (Higgsfield)

| Plan | Credits/mo | Rough video yield |
|---|---|---|
| Basic | 120 | ~15 standard clips |
| Pro | 600 | ~75 standard clips |
| Max | 1,800 | ~225 standard clips |

Model tiers: Free (Soul 2.0, DoP Lite) · Low (0.1–2 credits) · Mid (2–10) · Premium (10+). A standard Kling clip runs ~8 credits; premium/longer/Cinema Studio sessions cost more.

Going direct to Kling: ~$0.084/sec at 720p standard, ~$0.112/sec pro, ~$0.42/sec native 4K. Credits **reset each billing cycle and don't roll over** — schedule production so paid credits don't evaporate.

## The no-guess pipeline (credit-saving order of operations)

1. **Write the shot list first.** Every clip planned before a single credit is spent.
2. **Draft cheap.** Turbo/Lite models for composition and motion tests.
3. **Render heroes expensive.** Premium models only for faces, dialogue, and key story beats.
4. **One clip at a time, quality-gated.** A failed clip never chains — re-prompt, don't hope.
5. **Price before you send.** Estimate cost per request before batching; verify balance before a batch, not after.

## Where to spend vs save

- **Spend:** hero close-ups, dialogue shots, the trailer moment, the final shot.
- **Save:** establishers, B-roll, transitions, montages — Turbo is fine.
- **Free tools that don't look free:** CapCut for color/LUTs/grain, stabilization in post instead of re-rendering, compositing fixes (face swaps from close shots) instead of regenerating wide shots.

## The short-film budget frame

A 3–5 minute festival film at ~4 seconds per shot is 45–75 shots. At draft-then-hero discipline, most shots need 2–4 generations to land. Budget for 150–300 generations and plan the credit pool before starting — or split across platforms by shot type.

## Per-clip costs across platforms (third-party estimates, Oct 2026 — re-verify before budgeting)

| Platform | Est. cost per clip | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Vidu | ~$0.05 | Cheapest; free tier non-commercial |
| PixVerse | ~$0.07 | Budget pick |
| Pika | ~$0.17–0.61 | Standard plan has NO commercial use — trap |
| Hailuo (MiniMax) | ~$0.44–0.76 | Best price/quality ratio per multiple sources |
| Luma | ~$0.30–1.20 | |
| Kling 3.0 | ~$0.40 | Strong motion/camera control |
| Veo 3.1 Fast | ~$0.40–0.50 | Native audio; cheapest premium-quality route |
| Runway Gen-4.5 | ~$1.44–1.50 | Fastest generation |
| Higgsfield (Seedance 2.5) | ~$2.48 | Aggregates many models |
| Sora 2 | ~$0.40–2.00 | Longest clips (up to 25s) |

## Rules of thumb from working filmmakers

- **~$80 per finished minute** of film, all-in.
- **3–5 takes per keeper; 2–5x raw-to-finished multiplier.** Budget the rejects, not the hero renders.
- **$40–165 in credits** for a disciplined 3-minute short; $150–300+ without discipline.
- **Resolution ladder:** 480p drafts → 720/1080p heroes → upscale to 4K in post (native 4K ≈ $1/sec).
- **Audio-first:** lock voiceover/soundtrack before generating video — cheap audio prevents expensive timing-mismatch re-rolls.
- **Cautionary:** one documented Higgsfield pilot burned ~$260,000 in credits over 4 days for ~8 usable shots — brute-force iteration without craft. The no-guess rule exists because of math like this.

## Try it

Run your numbers in the [interactive budget calculator](../budget.html) — runtime, shot length, model, and discipline in, cost envelope out.

# Competition teardowns

Shot-by-shot craft lessons from films that placed in judged AI-film competitions. Every entry below was found with an attributed source — nothing invented. Items the research could not verify are flagged.

## The pattern before the films

Across Runway AIFF, Project Odyssey, Reply AIFF, the Higgsfield Action Contest, and MIT's hackathon, judges reward the same things: **story over spectacle, authorial intent, character/POV discipline, originality, sound design, and polish as the floor.** They punish: visible morphing/inconsistency, generic "AI slop," tech demos without narrative, and AI that pulls focus from the story.

Distilled: narrative cohesion + committed POV + intentional AI use + pro-grade sound + consistent visuals. Originality is the tiebreaker; polish is the entry ticket.

## The case studies

### "Total Pixel Space" — Jacob Adler, Runway AIFF 2025 Grand Prix
9:28 essay film. A voiceover calculates how many possible images could exist in digital space; surreal tableaux illustrate it. Inspired by Borges' "The Library of Babel." Tools: image generators + synthetic voices + Runway Gen-3; over a year in production, tens of thousands of images. Field: ~6,000 submissions; judges included Harmony Korine and Gaspar Noé.
**Why it won:** concept-first, AI-thematic — the medium is the message. The critic's take: it treats AI's glitches and eeriness as material to think with, carried by old-fashioned style and narrative. **Steal:** make the film *about* what the medium does, or make the medium invisible — never halfway.

### "Get Me Out" — Daniel Antebi, Runway AIFF 2024 Grand Prix
6 min. Aka flees a shadowy suburban house that stores his haunting memories, embodied by a blood-red figure of pure muscle. About displacement and mental health. Tools: Luma (3D environment capture), Runway video-to-video, ComfyUI (rotoscoped a performer, re-skinned him as muscle).
**Why it won:** hybrid craft — live-action emotional performance with invisible, motivated AI VFX. Antebi's own read: the artist-jurors resonated with the storytelling, not the tool cleverness. **Steal:** shoot the emotion for real; use AI only for what the budget couldn't do otherwise.

### "A Face Only a Mother Could Love" — Robert Gaudette, Runway AIFF 2026 Grand Prix + Reply AIFF 2026 winner
Photorealistic short: Marcel, a solitary Parisian dancer born with facial disfigurement; a woman's approach sparks connection. Tools: Grok, Nano Banana, Seedance — chosen, in his words, as the only viable way to film the screenplay without budget, cast, or crew. It started as an old screenplay experiment, never meant for festivals.
**Why it won:** intimacy and POV — tight shots establishing point of view in a way reviewers don't associate with AI imagery; nothing read as slop. **Steal:** a real screenplay beats a prompt. Character-first photorealism is now a proven winning lane.

### "GRANDMA vs WASP" — Muhannad Nassar & Simon Meyer, Higgsfield Action Contest winner
Action short. The duo never met in person — async remote workflow across time zones in Higgsfield's Cinema Studio. Field: 8,752 submissions, 139 countries. Judges (Jason Zada, Buralqy, Jama Jurabaev) prioritized storytelling and directorial intent over technical polish.
**Why it won:** proof that decentralized AI production works — two strangers, one film, no studio. **Steal:** team up across disciplines; judges reward directorial intent, not solo prompt heroics.

### "CUPID" — Nikolay Shestak, Higgsfield Action Contest finalist
Tagline: "Aggression has become the norm. It's time for silence." Shestak is an established actor/filmmaker using Higgsfield for concepts that would need prohibitive traditional budgets.
**Why it won:** the archetype judges love — a professional using AI for impossible scale, not novelty. **Steal:** bring a filmmaker's eye; the tool is the budget, not the idea.

### "SCRATCH" — Ash & Aram Gevorkyan, Higgsfield Action Contest finalist
High-production-value action short/trailer, made in **five days** by a director/musician + 3D/VFX generalist duo. Early Higgsfield adopters with commercial music-video fluency. Audiences mistook it for a studio-backed theatrical trailer.
**Why it won:** deep tool fluency plus trailer-form craft — sound, cutting, pacing. **Steal:** five days of fluent execution beats five weeks of hesitant prompting. Learn the tool until it's invisible.

### "One Last Wish" — Project Odyssey S2 Narrative Gold
An elderly inmate's final wish. Made in **48 hours** at a Norwegian AI-film workshop: a real screenwriter's script, a director, a dedicated AI-visuals artist, and a dedicated editor/sound designer.
**Why it won:** professional division of labor. A real script plus dedicated edit and sound beat solo prompting in the narrative category. **Steal:** split the roles even on a tiny team — never let the prompter also be the sound designer.

### "Le Drip" — Alex Naghavi & Ezra Li, Reply AIFF 2026 2nd
Animated short: a fish's final day on Earth, rendered as living oil paintings — dense textured brushstrokes moving across the screen.
**Why it placed:** a committed, authored art style instead of chasing photorealism. **Steal:** a strong style is a consistency strategy — painterly motion hides the seams photorealism exposes.

### "Jailbird" — Andrew Salter, Runway AIFF 2025 2nd
A chicken's journey — from the bird's POV — to a UK prison to join a rehabilitation program. Absurdist comedy in a 6,000-entry field.
**Why it placed:** high-concept premise plus total POV discipline. **Steal:** bold premise + locked POV stands out more than another beautiful drifting landscape.

### "Generation" — Riccardo Fusetti, Runway AIFF 2023 Grand Prix (inaugural)
Contemporary dance/performance fused with massive VFX and philosophical voiceover (Gen-1-era restyle).
**Why it won:** expressive, bold mixed-media authorship carried it in the festival's first year. **Steal:** performance plus stylization is a durable formula — the human body gives AI imagery something to hold onto.

### Also noted
"Centenarian Kindergarten" (2xLabs, Reply 2026 3rd + AI-for-Good), "The Child of the Sea" (Ibai Abad, Reply special mention — tactile stop-motion universe on an impossible budget), "For Pixi" (NYU team, MIT Hackathon Best Character), "DO NOT DISTURB THE SANE MAN" (Odyssey S2 Open Format Gold), and AAIFF 2026 winners from 8,067 entries across 125 countries.

## The cautionary case

A much-hyped contest winner was panned for three-eyed cyclopses, size-shifting characters, and feet-for-hands. Press called it a showcase of AI filmmaking's current limits. **Lesson: no hype forgives broken continuity. Consistency is the floor, not the ceiling.**

## What to steal — the winner's checklist

- [ ] A real story with a turn — not a vibe reel
- [ ] AI invisible, or the film is *about* AI imagery — never halfway
- [ ] Committed POV held across every shot
- [ ] Sound designed like a film, not a slideshow (custom music, real voice actors, layered foley)
- [ ] Zero visible morphing — consistency is the entry ticket
- [ ] Human craft felt on screen: a script, an edit, a mix — not just prompts

- https://venturebeat.com/ai/runways-la-film-festival-marked-an-inflection-point-for-ai-movies

<!-- chapter: case-studies/entry-craft-teardowns.md -->
# Entry Craft Teardowns: How the Winning Films Were Actually Made

The companion chapter lists *what placed and why*. This one is the *how* — the production techniques behind judged entries, broken into steps you can copy. Every teardown follows the same shape: **the technique**, **the craft principle**, **copy it** (actionable steps), and the **budget/time footprint** where it's documented.

## 1. The async remote workflow — "GRANDMA vs WASP" ($150K, Higgsfield Action Contest)

**The technique.** Directors Muhannad Nassar and Simon Meyer never met in person. They built the film async across time zones inside Higgsfield's Cinema Studio — one shared project where generations, prompts, and assets were all visible to both collaborators. No studio, no set, no shoot days; the "set" was a shared generation window.

**The craft principle.** Judges (Jason Zada, Buralqy, Jama Jurabaev) said they prioritized storytelling and directorial intent over technical polish — in a field of 8,752 submissions from 139 countries. The remote workflow won because the *directing* was centralized even though the *labor* was distributed: one vision, two executors, zero drift between them.

**Copy it.**
- Write a one-page director's intent doc before generating anything: logline, tone references, the single emotion each act must land.
- Work in a shared project, not DMs — every prompt, generation, and select lives where your collaborator can see and fork it.
- Split by discipline, not by scene: one person owns performance/character, the other owns camera/action. Review each other's selects daily.
- Lock a style bible on day one (one style line, aspect ratio, grain/grade, lens language) so two people can't drift apart.

**Footprint.** Two people, zero travel, consumer AI subscriptions. The budget went to time, not gear.

## 2. The five-day sprint — "SCRATCH" ($50K, Higgsfield Action Contest)

**The technique.** Director/musician Ash Gevorkyan + 3D/VFX generalist Aram Gevorkyan made a trailer-grade action short in five days. Audiences mistook it for a studio-backed theatrical trailer. The weapon was trailer form: sound, cutting, and pacing doing the heavy lifting while the imagery stayed in short, high-energy bursts that never linger long enough to break.

**The craft principle.** Fluency beats time. Five days of fluent execution beats five weeks of hesitant prompting — because the duo already knew their tools cold, every generation was a deliberate choice, not an experiment.

**Copy it.**
- Cut a trailer, not a short: 60–90 seconds, three acts (hook / escalation / title card), music-driven pacing.
- Keep shots short (2–4 seconds). Short shots hide consistency breaks; long takes expose them.
- Build the sound design first or in parallel — trailer percussion, risers, and hard-hitting SFX sell "studio" more than any pixel does.
- Budget generations per shot: 3–5 variations for hero shots, 1–2 for connective tissue. Decide selects fast.

**Footprint.** Five days, two specialists, deep tool fluency. The most replicable winning formula in this chapter.

## 3. The hybrid pipeline — "Passport Rush" and "Get Me Out"

**The technique.** "Passport Rush" combined hand-drawn storyboards + Blender previz + AI animation, publishing every prompt and asset. "Get Me Out" (Runway AIFF 2024 Grand Prix) captured a real 3D environment in Luma, shot a real performer, then used Runway video-to-video and ComfyUI to rotoscope and re-skin him as a blood-red muscle figure.

**The craft principle.** Shoot the emotion for real; use AI only for what the budget couldn't do otherwise. Both films put a human performance or human draftsmanship at the center and used AI as the *impossible* layer — never the *entire* layer. Jurors (working artists, in Antebi's case) resonated with the storytelling, not the tool cleverness.

**Copy it.**
- Board on paper or in Blender first. If the story doesn't work as boards, it won't work as generations.
- Capture or shoot anything with a human body in it for real — even a phone previz gives the AI motion something truthful to hold onto.
- Use video-to-video / motion transfer for transformation, not text-to-video for invention. Transforming real motion beats inventing motion.
- Keep one "truth anchor" per scene (a real plate, a real performance, a real drawing) and let AI handle the other 80%.

**Footprint.** "Get Me Out" was a solo-plus-tools production; "Passport Rush" published its full pipeline as a teaching resource. Both prove hybrid beats pure-generation for emotional weight.

## 4. The authored-style strategy — "Le Drip," "The Tale of the Peony," "The Child of the Sea"

**The technique.** "Le Drip" (Reply AIFF 2026 2nd) rendered a fish's final day as living oil paintings — dense textured brushstrokes in motion. "The Tale of the Peony" (MEGA 2026 Best AI Short) used AI keyframe animation + rice-paper texture + manual keyframe refinement. "The Child of the Sea" built a tactile stop-motion universe.

**The craft principle.** A strong, committed art style is a *consistency strategy*. Painterly motion, rice-paper grain, and stop-motion stepping all hide the seams that photorealism exposes. Judges reward authored intent: pick a lane and commit so hard the style becomes the film's identity.

**Copy it.**
- Choose your style for what it *forgives*, not just what it looks like. Ask: "what breaks when this style drifts 5%?" If the answer is "nothing visible," it's a good judged-category style.
- Lock the style in one sentence and put it verbatim in every prompt ([STYLE] block discipline).
- Add the texture in a separate pass: film grain, paper texture, brushstroke overlays in post unify generations from different models.
- For stylized work, use the animated prompt register — no lens or DOF language (see `prompt-engineering.md`).

**Footprint.** Style commitment costs nothing in credits and buys the most consistency per dollar of any technique here.

## 5. The photoreal character piece — "A Face Only a Mother Could Love" (Runway AIFF 2026 Grand Prix + Reply AIFF 2026)

**The technique.** Robert Gaudette started with an old screenplay — a real script about Marcel, a solitary Parisian dancer — and chose Grok, Nano Banana, and Seedance as, in his words, the only viable way to film it without budget, cast, or crew. Tight shots established point of view in a way reviewers don't associate with AI imagery.

**The craft principle.** A real screenplay beats a prompt. Character-first photorealism with locked POV is now a proven winning lane: intimacy and perspective discipline make AI imagery read as *cinema* instead of *demo*.

**Copy it.**
- Write (or adapt) a real script first — dialogue, beats, turns. If it works on the page, the AI only has to execute.
- Hold one POV ruthlessly. Every shot should answer "whose eyes are we in?" before "what does it look like?"
- Favor tight shots over wides for character pieces: close-ups carry performance; wides expose geometry the models can't hold.
- Cast the models to the job: photoreal portrait models for faces, motion-strong models for body movement — don't ask one model to do both.

**Footprint.** One filmmaker, a screenplay, three models. Proof that writing is the cheapest VFX.

## 6. The long-form discipline — "Oneiric" (20 min) and "Total Pixel Space" (9:28, Runway AIFF 2025 Grand Prix)

**The technique.** "Oneiric" ran a 20-minute drama through Cinema Studio with open-sourced everything: every Seedance asset and prompt, Claude skills for scripting/acting/prompting, a color-coded Diagram Skill frame map tracking every shot, and a consistent-lens-look trick for visual unity. (Correction: earlier versions of this guide repeated a "Cannes premiere" claim for Oneiric — dedicated research found no source for it. It was made for Higgsfield's own film festival; the Cannes-adjacent screening was *Hell Grind's*, a third-party industry showcase, not an official selection.) "Total Pixel Space" spent over a year in production generating tens of thousands of images for a 9-minute essay film.

**The craft principle.** Long-form AI filmmaking is *asset management*, not prompting. The winners built production systems — frame maps, skill libraries, lens-look rules — that let hundreds of generations cohere. Time in pre-production and systems pays back exponentially at 10+ minutes.

**Copy it.**
- Build a frame map before generating: every shot on a timeline with its lens, lighting, and character state, color-coded by status.
- Separate identity from motion in every prompt (Identity Block vs Motion Block) — at feature length, this is the difference between a cast and a crowd of strangers.
- Validate at 720p, upscale only winners. At long-form scale, rendering everything at max quality first is how budgets die.
- Re-anchor references every few generations — don't wait for drift to become visible.
- Use J/L cuts and a shared ambience bed to mask transitions; sound covers a multitude of visual sins.

**Footprint.** "Oneiric" was a small team with systems; "Total Pixel Space" was a year of iteration. Both show that long-form is a marathon budgeted in *organization*, not just credits. (Full long-form pipelines get their own chapter in `craft/long-form-pipeline.md`.)

## 7. The floor — what kills entries

The cautionary case: a hyped contest winner had three-eyed cyclopses, size-shifting characters, and feet-for-hands. Press called it a showcase of AI filmmaking's current limits. **No hype forgives broken continuity.** Across every festival in the companion chapter, judges punish the same things: visible morphing, generic AI slop, tech demos without narrative, and AI that pulls focus from the story.

**Copy it (in reverse).** Before submitting, run the entry-killer audit:
- [ ] No morphing faces, extra limbs, or shifting wardrobe across cuts
- [ ] No shot exists just to show off a model — every shot serves the story
- [ ] Sound designed like a film (custom music, voice, layered foley), not a slideshow
- [ ] One committed POV or style held across the entire runtime
- [ ] A human edit: pacing, turns, and a button image — not a prompt sequence

## Build your entry like a winner — assembly order

1. **Script first.** A real story with a turn. (Teardowns 5, 6)
2. **Pick your consistency strategy.** Authored style, hybrid truth-anchor, or photoreal POV discipline — choose for what it forgives. (Teardowns 3, 4, 5)
3. **Lock the style bible.** One style line, verbatim, in every prompt. (Teardowns 1, 4)
4. **Board or previz.** Paper, Blender, or phone footage — prove the story before spending credits. (Teardown 3)
5. **Generate in the right order.** Keyframes → motion → selects; 720p drafts, upscale winners only. (Teardown 6)
6. **Cut like a trailer editor.** Short shots, music-driven pacing, J/L cuts. (Teardown 2)
7. **Sound is half the film.** Custom music, real or AI voices with rights, layered foley, ambience bed. (Teardowns 2, 6)
8. **Run the entry-killer audit.** Zero morphing, zero demo shots, committed POV throughout. (Teardown 7)
